direction.comments: The direction on a macroscale is genuinely claustrophobic, playing like a horror movie or psychological thriller, as the Academy ratio, wide-angle lenses, and close-up shots of faces make you feel trapped, like you're in jail with Elizabeth Holmes and her family, building this claustrophobic world where you're stuck with Elizabeth Holmes and the lies of this family, while also feeling auteur-esque, as if it were directed like PT Anderson's The Master; the direction on a microscale is so Nathan Fielder-esque while still feeling like a horror movie, as Nathan Fielder, a top-notch visionary of our time who graduated from one of Canada's top business schools with really good grades for a reason, uses his deadpan Nathan Fielder shtick to bring out comedy while keeping the movie serious and tense; the storytelling is a major reason why I can rate this movie, as it genuinely feels like a narrative, like they made a movie through a documentary; the tension is built so well that the whole movie genuinely feels like the opening sequence of Inglourious Basterds, where Hans Landa slowly corners the farmer hiding a family under the floorboards, keeping you on your toes and uneasy for three hours as the sound makes it feel like a horror movie, almost like The Silence of the Lambs or The Shining

performance.comments: She says she's not putting on a character, but it very much feels like she's putting on a character
His name is Nathan Fielder, and he graduated from one of Canada's top business schools with really good grades
Genuinely might be the best performance I've seen from them, as they are able to work in the rehearsal moments and work with Nathan Fielder to help tell the story

cast.comments: It's a documentary, so you can't really grade the acting

story.comments: The concept is genuinely amazing, playing like an episode of The Rehearsal but for Elizabeth Holmes and her husband, as Nathan Fielder inserts himself into the scenario and documents it, and while it's mostly factual, the way they handle the rehearsal segments is phenomenal, so go in blind; the plot structure is split into two halves, with the first half following Elizabeth Holmes during her final 34 days before she goes to prison, and the second half following life two years later through the chaos of her husband, his narcissism, and how he's using Elizabeth Holmes to benefit himself, and the way they turn him into the villain of the movie is top-notch; character writing doesn't really apply to a documentary, but the way they paint Elizabeth Holmes as someone you can somewhat empathize with while knowing she's a terrible person for the most part, along with how they paint her husband, the mystery character they bring in, and Nathan Fielder's attachment to it all, makes it feel like a narrative

screenplay.comments: The dialogue shows that Nathan Fielder is the right person for this job, as he is super serious when he needs to be in his conversations with Elizabeth Holmes and her husband; the humor comes from Nathan Fielder being a comedian at the end of the day, as he's able to bring out comedy in the moment, making it feel like The Rehearsal; the symbolism is top-notch, showing the deceit and lying nature of these tech entrepreneurs, who are pathological liars and narcissists that defraud people and even try to lie to Nathan Fielder, all leading to the powerful message at the end of 'who do you believe,' since people can always manipulate the truth, which is what Elizabeth Holmes did, what her husband is doing, and to an extent, what Nathan Fielder is doing by making a narrative through a documentary; the foreshadowing is good and well made for a documentary, helping it genuinely feel like a narrative

score.comments: Makes the documentary feel like a psychological thriller, aiding the tension and tone of the movie; it is well composed and keeps you uneasy

cinematography.comments: Phenomenal, as shooting in the Academy ratio while mixing wide-angle shots with close-up shots of faces makes you feel so claustrophobic, like you're trapped with Elizabeth Holmes, her husband, and her family, and it genuinely feels like an auteur film, like a PT Anderson movie, The Shining, or a Yorgos Lanthimos movie, even though it's a documentary

editing.comments: The slow pans and slow zooms in on subjects, along with how the reveals happen mid-conversation, add to both the comedy and the shock factor, and the editing and cinematography work hand in hand as characters in themselves that help tell the story

sound.comments: Chilling, making you so tense and making this documentary feel like a psychological thriller

production_design.comments: Mostly shot in one house, and the movie was also shot in Austin, especially the second half, which makes it feel very close to home since it shows places I've been; it's wild to think I could have run into Nathan Fielder in Austin

makeup.comments: Used for the rehearsal sequences to help make them feel like the real world

costumes.comments: Used for the rehearsal sequences to help make them feel like the real world

review.pacing: Pretty slow and a bit bloated, with a lot of shots that go on a little too long, so it very much feels like a three-hour documentary, but the pacing adds to the feeling of being stuck with these characters, making the movie feel chilling and hammering home the points it's trying to make, even if it is very long; with the movie being a bit repetitive, you could've maybe cut 20 minutes in the middle of the movie
review.climax: Phenomenal, as the final hour brings the movie together and makes up for the lulls in the middle hour, with the final 20 minutes especially tying everything together in a truly shocking way that sticks the landing very well
review.tone: Feels like Nathan Fielder directed an episode of The Rehearsal like it was The Shining, as it's chilling, scary, and funny since Nathan Fielder is a comedian at the end of the day, making it almost the perfect documentary because it feels so much like a narrative
review.final_notes: I usually don't rate documentaries because I find them hard to rate, but I'm making an exception for this movie because it really is a narrative
review.overall: Overall, 'You Can See Everything' is phenomenal and genuinely one of the best documentaries I've ever seen; it feels like Nathan Fielder directed an episode of The Rehearsal like it was The Shining, making it so tense and jaw-dropping, and while I usually don't rate documentaries, I'm making an exception for this one because it really is a narrative, with captivating storytelling, claustrophobic cinematography, and deadpan comedy to deliver a sight you can't unsee
